questions.question: Which statement best describes "narrow AI"?

options.A: AI that can perform any intellectual task a human can
options.B: AI designed and trained to perform a specific task or a narrow range of tasks
options.C: AI that is aware of its own existence
options.D: AI that only runs on specialised hardware

questions.explanation: Narrow (or weak) AI is built for a specific task, such as image classification or spam filtering. General AI, which would match human breadth of capability, does not yet exist.

questions.question: What is a common characteristic that makes many AI-based systems difficult to test compared with conventional software?

options.A: They are always written in Python
options.B: Their expected results can be hard to define precisely, creating a test oracle problem

questions.explanation: For many AI-based systems the exact correct output is not known in advance, so testers face a test oracle problem and must use partial or heuristic oracles.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of generative AI?

options.A: A decision tree that predicts loan default (yes/no)
options.B: A large language model that produces a paragraph of new text from a prompt
options.C: A linear regression model that forecasts a house price
options.D: A rule-based engine that validates form fields

questions.explanation: Generative AI creates new content (text, images, audio, code). Classification and regression models produce labels or numeric predictions rather than new artefacts.

questions.question: In the context of AI-based systems, what does "non-determinism" mean?

options.A: The system has no source code
options.B: The same input can produce different outputs on different runs
options.D: The system cannot be deployed to production

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic AI systems may return different results for identical inputs, for example because of sampling in a language model or ongoing online learning.

questions.question: Which risk-tier concept is introduced by the EU AI Act?

options.A: Systems are graded by lines of code
options.B: AI systems are categorised by risk level, with stricter obligations for high-risk uses
options.C: All AI systems are banned by default

questions.explanation: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based approach: unacceptable-risk uses are prohibited, high-risk uses carry strict requirements, and limited/minimal-risk uses have lighter obligations.

questions.question: Which term describes an AI system that continues to learn and change its behaviour after deployment based on new data?

options.A: Locked system
options.B: Self-learning (adaptive) system

questions.explanation: A self-learning or adaptive system updates its model in operation. A locked system keeps the same model until an explicit, controlled update is released.

questions.question: Why is specialised hardware such as GPUs often used for AI workloads?

options.A: It removes the need for any testing
options.B: It accelerates the large volume of parallel matrix computations used in training and inference
options.C: It guarantees the model is unbiased

questions.explanation: Neural network training and inference rely on massive parallel linear algebra, which GPUs, TPUs and similar accelerators execute far faster than general-purpose CPUs.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically considered a technology used to implement AI-based systems?

options.A: Machine learning
options.B: Rule-based / expert systems
options.D: Manual data entry into a spreadsheet

questions.explanation: AI is implemented with techniques such as machine learning, knowledge-based/expert systems, search, and fuzzy logic. Manual spreadsheet data entry is not an AI technique.

questions.question: What does "AI effect" refer to?

options.A: The tendency for a capability to stop being called "AI" once it becomes common and well understood
options.B: The visual output produced by a generative model
options.C: The electricity consumed by a data centre
options.D: The improvement in accuracy after fine-tuning

questions.explanation: The AI effect describes how, once a technique becomes routine (for example optical character recognition), people often stop regarding it as "real" AI.

questions.question: Which quality characteristic describes an AI-based system's ability to keep performing correctly when given unexpected or noisy inputs?

options.A: Portability
options.B: Robustness

questions.explanation: Robustness is the degree to which a system continues to function correctly in the presence of invalid inputs, stressful conditions, or adversarial perturbations.

questions.question: What is "algorithmic bias" in an AI-based system?

options.A: A preference for a particular programming language
options.B: Systematic and unfair discrimination in outputs against certain groups or attributes
options.C: A rounding error in floating-point arithmetic
options.D: A slow response time under load

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias is a systematic error that produces unfair outcomes, often arising from unrepresentative training data or from proxies for protected attributes.

questions.question: Which quality characteristic is concerned with a human being able to take over control from an AI-based system when needed?

options.A: Transparency
options.B: User controllability (intervenability)

questions.explanation: User controllability, sometimes called intervenability, is the ability for humans to intervene in or override the behaviour of an AI-based system.

questions.question: "Explainability" of an AI-based system primarily means:

options.A: The system runs quickly
options.B: The reasons for a system's output can be understood by humans

questions.explanation: Explainability is the degree to which the behaviour or a specific output of an AI system can be understood and explained in human terms.

questions.question: Which standard provides an AI-specific quality model that extends ISO/IEC 25010?

options.A: ISO/IEC 25059
options.B: ISO 9001

questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 25059 defines a quality model for AI systems, adding AI-specific characteristics such as functional adaptability, robustness, transparency, and intervenability.

questions.question: "Autonomy" as an AI quality characteristic refers to the system's ability to:

options.A: Operate for periods without human oversight or intervention
options.B: Run without electricity
options.C: Be installed on any operating system

questions.explanation: Autonomy is the degree to which an AI-based system can operate independently of human control for a given period and context.

questions.question: Why is "flexibility / adaptability" both a benefit and a testing challenge for AI-based systems?

options.A: It never changes the model
options.B: The system can adjust to new situations, but that same change of behaviour must be re-verified
options.C: It only affects the user interface colours
options.D: It removes the need for regression testing

questions.explanation: Adaptability lets a system handle situations outside its original specification, but any behavioural change introduces new risk that must be tested again.

questions.question: In supervised learning, the training data consists of:

options.A: Inputs only
options.B: Inputs paired with known correct outputs (labels)
options.C: Rewards and penalties from an environment

questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labelled examples so the model learns a mapping from inputs to the provided target outputs.

questions.question: Which ML task assigns each input to one of a fixed set of categories?

options.A: Regression
options.B: Classification

questions.explanation: Classification predicts a discrete class label. Regression predicts a continuous value, and clustering groups data without predefined labels.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the validation dataset during ML development?

options.A: To train the model's weights
options.B: To tune hyperparameters and compare models without touching the final test set
options.C: To be delivered to the customer

questions.explanation: The validation set guides model and hyperparameter selection. The test set is held back for a final, unbiased estimate of performance.

questions.question: Overfitting occurs when a model:

options.A: Performs poorly on both training and test data
options.B: Learns the training data (including its noise) so closely that it generalises poorly to new data
options.C: Has too few parameters to learn anything
options.D: Is trained on too much data

questions.explanation: An overfitted model fits training noise and idiosyncrasies, giving high training accuracy but low accuracy on unseen data.

questions.question: Which of the following is a hyperparameter rather than a learned parameter?

options.A: The weights of a neural network
options.B: The learning rate used during training
options.C: The bias terms of a linear model
options.D: The embedding vectors produced by training

questions.explanation: Hyperparameters such as learning rate, number of layers, or tree depth are set before training. Weights and biases are learned from the data.

questions.question: In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by:

options.A: Being given labelled input/output pairs
options.B: Interacting with an environment and receiving rewards or penalties

questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning optimises a policy through trial and error, using a reward signal from the environment as feedback.

questions.question: What does "unsupervised learning" primarily aim to do?

options.A: Predict labelled outcomes
options.B: Discover structure or patterns in data that has no labels
options.D: Fine-tune a language model with human feedback

questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning, for example clustering or association rule mining, finds patterns in unlabelled data.

questions.question: "Transfer learning" means:

options.A: Copying test cases between projects
options.B: Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a related task
options.D: Converting a model to another file format

questions.explanation: Transfer learning starts from a model pretrained on a large general dataset and adapts it (often by fine-tuning) to a specific downstream task with less data.

questions.question: Which statement about a confusion matrix is correct?

options.A: It shows counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives
options.B: It lists the model's hyperparameters
options.C: It records training time per epoch
options.D: It plots the learning rate schedule

questions.explanation: A confusion matrix cross-tabulates predicted versus actual classes, giving the TP, FP, TN, and FN counts used to compute metrics such as precision and recall.

questions.question: Recall (sensitivity) of a classifier measures:

options.A: The proportion of actual positives that the model correctly identifies
options.B: The proportion of predicted positives that are correct
options.C: The overall fraction of correct predictions
options.D: The time to score one input

questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all real positive cases, how many did the model catch. Precision is TP / (TP + FP).

questions.question: The F1-score is:

options.A: The arithmetic mean of accuracy and recall
options.B: The harmonic mean of precision and recall
options.C: The area under the ROC curve

questions.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving a single balanced figure that is low if either precision or recall is low.

questions.question: Why can "accuracy" be a misleading metric for a highly imbalanced classification problem?

options.A: It is impossible to compute
options.B: A model can score high accuracy simply by always predicting the majority class

questions.explanation: With, say, 99% negatives, predicting "negative" every time gives 99% accuracy while catching no positives, so precision, recall and F1 are needed instead.

questions.question: In the ML workflow, "feature engineering" refers to:

options.A: Writing user stories for features of the application
options.B: Selecting, transforming, or constructing input variables so the model can learn effectively

questions.explanation: Feature engineering prepares raw data into informative inputs, for example scaling, encoding categories, or deriving ratios.

questions.question: A pretrained large language model that is adapted to a company's support tickets using additional training is said to be:

options.A: Clustered
options.B: Fine-tuned

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on domain-specific data so it adapts to that domain's language and tasks.

questions.question: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves an LLM's answers by:

options.A: Increasing the model's temperature
options.B: Retrieving relevant documents at query time and adding them to the prompt as context
options.D: Training the model from scratch on every request

questions.explanation: RAG grounds generation in retrieved, up-to-date source material, reducing hallucination and letting the model cite information it was not trained on.

questions.question: Which of these is a typical measure of ML functional performance for a regression model?

options.A: Precision
options.B: Mean absolute error (MAE)

questions.explanation: Regression models are evaluated with error measures such as MAE, MSE, RMSE, or R-squared. Precision, recall, F1 and confusion matrices apply to classification.

questions.question: The "test oracle problem" for AI-based systems is that:

options.A: There are no test tools available
options.B: It is difficult to determine the expected result for a given input

questions.explanation: Without a reliable oracle, testers cannot simply compare actual to expected output and must use pseudo-oracles, metamorphic relations, or acceptable-range checks.

questions.question: Metamorphic testing is useful for AI-based systems because it:

options.A: Requires the exact expected output for every input
options.B: Checks relationships between the outputs of related inputs instead of exact values
options.D: Replaces the need for test data

questions.explanation: A metamorphic relation states how the output should change (or stay the same) when the input is transformed, so it works even when no single expected value is known.

questions.question: An "adversarial example" is:

options.A: A test case written by a competitor
options.B: An input with small, deliberate perturbations that cause the model to produce a wrong output

questions.explanation: Adversarial examples exploit model sensitivity: a perturbation imperceptible to humans can flip a classifier's prediction, which is a robustness and security concern.

questions.question: "Red teaming" a generative AI system means:

options.A: Reviewing the training code for style issues
options.B: Deliberately attempting to make the system produce harmful, unsafe, or policy-violating output
options.C: Load testing with many concurrent users
options.D: Checking the colour scheme of the UI

questions.explanation: Red teaming probes a GenAI system with adversarial prompts and jailbreak attempts to find safety, security and misuse weaknesses before release.

questions.question: Why is exploratory testing valuable for AI-based systems?

options.A: It guarantees 100% requirements coverage
options.B: It lets testers investigate unexpected or emergent behaviour that scripted tests may miss
options.C: It removes the need for test data

questions.explanation: AI systems can behave in ways that were not specified. Exploratory testing uses tester insight to probe those areas interactively.

questions.question: A "locked" ML system is easier to test than a self-learning one mainly because:

options.A: It has no defects
options.B: Its behaviour does not change between the test environment and production

questions.explanation: With a locked model the version tested is the version released, so test results remain valid. A self-learning model may drift after deployment.

questions.question: Which of the following is a pseudo-oracle approach?

options.A: Comparing the system output against the output of an independently built implementation of the same function
options.B: Skipping verification entirely
options.C: Running the same test twice on the same build

questions.explanation: A pseudo-oracle (for example back-to-back testing against a reference implementation) provides an approximate expected result when a true oracle is unavailable.

questions.question: "Automation bias" during testing of an AI-based system refers to:

options.A: A tester over-trusting the system's output and failing to challenge incorrect results
options.B: A build server running out of disk space
options.D: A flaky test that fails intermittently

questions.explanation: Automation bias is the human tendency to accept machine-generated recommendations uncritically, which can let AI defects slip through review.

questions.question: When testing an AI-based system, a "partial oracle" might check that the output is:

options.A: Exactly one predetermined string
options.B: Within a plausible range or satisfies known constraints, even if the exact value is unknown

questions.explanation: A partial oracle verifies necessary properties (bounds, format, invariants) without needing the single correct answer.

questions.question: Which test level is specific to ML systems and focuses on the trained model in isolation?

options.A: Acceptance testing
options.B: Model testing

questions.explanation: CT-AI v2.0 treats input data testing and ML model testing as distinct test levels with their own risks and techniques.

questions.question: A key reason to involve testers early in an AI project is to:

options.A: Reduce the training dataset size
options.B: Help define measurable acceptance criteria and quality characteristics before the model is built

questions.explanation: Early tester involvement clarifies what "good enough" means (target metrics, fairness constraints, robustness expectations), which shapes data and model choices.

questions.question: Statistical testing of an AI-based system typically reports:

options.A: A simple pass or fail for a single input
options.B: Aggregate measures over many inputs, such as accuracy with a confidence interval

questions.explanation: Because individual predictions may be uncertain, AI test results are usually expressed statistically across a representative sample.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why is the quality of training data critical for an ML system?

options.A: Because the model can only be as good as the data it learns from
options.B: Because it changes the programming language used
options.C: Because it sets the screen resolution
options.D: Because it has no effect on the model

questions.explanation: Errors, gaps, or bias in training data are learned by the model. "Garbage in, garbage out" applies strongly to ML.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: "Data representativeness" means that the dataset:

options.A: Is stored in a relational database
options.B: Reflects the range and distribution of situations the model will meet in production

questions.explanation: If the training/test data does not match the operational data distribution, measured performance will not hold in production.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which of the following is a data-quality issue that input data testing looks for?

options.A: Duplicate records, missing values, and mislabelled examples
options.B: The number of GPUs in the cluster
options.C: The font used in the report

questions.explanation: Input data testing checks for completeness, accuracy, consistency, duplication, outliers, and label correctness.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: "Label noise" refers to:

options.A: Audio interference during recording
options.B: Incorrect target values assigned to training examples

questions.explanation: Label noise is annotation error. It confuses learning and also corrupts evaluation if it is present in the test set.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Disparate-impact analysis is used to detect:

options.A: Memory leaks
options.B: Whether outcomes differ unfairly across protected groups

questions.explanation: Disparate-impact analysis compares favourable-outcome rates between groups (for example by gender or ethnicity) to reveal potential discrimination.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A common cause of bias entering an ML model through data is:

options.A: Using a compiled language
options.B: Historical data that reflects past discriminatory decisions
options.C: Running tests on a CI server

questions.explanation: If historical labels encode biased human decisions, a model trained to reproduce them will perpetuate that bias.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why should the test dataset be kept separate and unseen during model training?

options.A: To save disk space
options.B: To give an unbiased estimate of how the model performs on new data (avoid data leakage)

questions.explanation: If test data influences training, evaluation results are optimistic. Strict separation prevents data leakage.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Data augmentation is primarily used to:

options.A: Delete rare classes
options.B: Create additional varied training examples (for example rotated or noised images) to improve robustness

questions.explanation: Augmentation synthesises plausible variations of existing data, expanding coverage and helping the model generalise.

questions.question: "Data drift" in a deployed ML system means:

options.A: The input data distribution in production changes over time compared with the training data
options.B: The database server moves to a new rack
options.D: The team changes its coding standard

questions.explanation: Data (covariate) drift is a change in the distribution of incoming features, which can silently degrade model performance.

questions.question: "Concept drift" refers to a change in:

options.A: The relationship between inputs and the target being predicted
options.B: The programming concept used in the codebase

questions.explanation: Concept drift means the underlying rule (P(y|x)) changes, so a previously accurate model becomes wrong even if the inputs look similar.

questions.question: Back-to-back testing of an ML model compares its output with:

options.A: A previous or alternative implementation used as a reference
options.B: The compiler version

questions.explanation: Back-to-back (differential) testing runs the same inputs through two implementations and flags disagreements for investigation.

questions.question: A/B testing of two model versions in production is used to:

options.A: Compare their real-world impact by routing live traffic to each and measuring outcomes
options.B: Alphabetically sort the training data

questions.explanation: A/B testing splits users between model A and model B and compares business or quality metrics to choose the better model.

questions.question: Underfitting is indicated when a model has:

options.A: High accuracy on training data but low on test data
options.B: Low accuracy on both training and test data

questions.explanation: Underfitting means the model is too simple or under-trained to capture the pattern, so it performs poorly even on the data it was trained on.

questions.question: Which coverage measure is specific to testing neural networks?

options.A: Statement coverage
options.B: Neuron coverage

questions.explanation: Neuron coverage (and variants like neuron-boundary or layer coverage) measures how much of a network's activation behaviour a test set exercises.

questions.question: "Shadow testing" (dark launch) of a new model means:

options.A: Running the new model on live inputs in parallel without acting on its outputs, to compare against the current model
options.B: Testing only at night

questions.explanation: Shadow deployment lets the candidate model score real traffic silently so its behaviour can be assessed before it takes over.

questions.question: Canary releasing of an ML model reduces risk by:

options.A: Sending the new model to a small subset of users first and monitoring before wider rollout
options.B: Training the model on canary images

questions.explanation: A canary release exposes the change to a limited population so problems are detected early and rollback is cheap.
